title: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
hook: beyond duty is the realm of knowledge: winds, waters, suns and worlds without number (Japji 35)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kete, so many, and your line, dharam khandd, the hinge between two realms. Today, through into the realm of knowledge.

Astronomers once pointed a space telescope at a tiny patch of sky that looked completely empty. Dark. Nothing there. They left the camera open a long time, collecting whatever faint light trickled in. When the picture came back, that empty patch was full of galaxies, each one a city of stars. A picture like that can make the floor drop away. The universe is bigger than anyone can hold in mind. Japji has a name for the place where that dizziness lives, and it got there with no telescope at all: the realm of knowledge.
screen: `AN EMPTY PATCH OF SKY.` → `FULL OF GALAXIES.` → `THE FLOOR DROPS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Gian Khand. In the first realm, you learn to live rightly on this earth. In the second, your eyes open to how big everything actually is. Nanak shows it by counting, and failing to finish. Kete, so many. So many winds, waters and fires. So many lands where deeds are done, so many great mountains. So many moons, so many suns, so many worlds and lands. He reaches for figures his listeners honored, the creator Brahma, Krishna, Shiva, the great teachers and sages, and says there are so many of them too. The point isn't to make anyone small. It's to show how big the whole is. Then the list turns to us: so many ways life begins, so many languages, so many kings, so many kinds of awareness, so many who serve. And the stanza ends: Nanak ant na ant. There is no end to its end. Knowledge here isn't a pile of facts. It's the moment the facts become too many to hold, and the heart goes quiet in wonder. Some Sikh teachers say this realm breaks the small self open: you can't stay the center of the world once you've seen how many worlds there are. In the stanza, that isn't a loss. It's where wonder starts.
screen: `GIAN KHAND — THE REALM OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `KETE — SO MANY SUNS, SO MANY WORLDS.` · `NANAK ANT NA ANT — NO END TO ITS END.` · `KNOWING, UNTIL WONDER TAKES OVER.` · then, large: `SO MANY WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture the room you're in, then the building, your town from above, the country, the whole earth turning, the sun and the other planets, the Milky Way, and galaxy after galaxy, so many. Don't try to hold it all; let it be too big, and notice whether feeling small is loss, or relief. Then come back to your breath, one breath in one body.
Gian Khand. The realm of knowledge, where your eyes open to so many winds, suns and worlds that the counting never ends. The second of Japji's five realms.
Your line: so many worlds. The counting never ends, and that is the point. Day two hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 is taught as the realm of knowledge, the second of the five khands, and its long list of kete, so many, is often read as the ego opening up before the vastness of creation.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the realm of knowledge, the second of Japji's five realms.

trapdoor: what you thought: the realm where smart people go.
what it means: the stage where your eyes open to the size of creation, and the small self loosens.
what a scholar hears: the stanza is built on kete, so many, repeated line after line, and closes on ant na ant, a phrase Japji uses for what can't be measured.

notes: Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original; the list is paraphrase and abbreviated. Macauliffe 1909 not quoted because not verified word for word.
Hubble Deep Field (1995): 'thousands of galaxies' in a patch of sky that looked empty; confirm the date and wording (commonly cited as about 3,000 galaxies, exposure over about ten days).

The stanza names Brahma, Krishna (kaan) and Shiva (mahes) as 'so many'; the script frames this as showing the size of creation, not diminishing anyone. Confirm the framing is respectful to Hindu listeners and faithful to Sikh commentary.
khaanee glossed as ways life begins (sources of creation) and baanee as languages or speech; confirm.
